hints: Notice that each equation is removing one electron from a gaseous positive ion, so think successive ionisation energy and what makes an electron harder to remove.
Check the electron arrangement left behind: Al3+, Si4+, P5+ and S6+ are all left with 10 electrons in a 1s2 2s2 2p6 neon-like core, so all lose the next electron from the n = 2 shell.
For isoelectronic ions losing an electron from the same shell, compare nuclear charge and existing positive charge to decide which nucleus pulls hardest.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the process as successive ionisation**

Each equation shows $X^{n+}(g) \rightarrow X^{(n+1)+}(g) + e^-$. This is an ionisation energy, and it is always endothermic because energy is needed to overcome attraction to the positive ion.

$$\text{1st, 2nd, 3rd... ionisation energy increases with charge}$$

**Find where the electron is removed from**

Write the starting ions. Al (Z=13), Si (Z=14), P (Z=15), S (Z=16) have all lost their n=3 outer electrons.

$$Al^{3+}, Si^{4+}, P^{5+}, S^{6+} = 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$$
All four are isoelectronic with neon, so the next electron comes from the n=2 shell in every case. There is no big jump to n=1 here to separate them.

**Compare nuclear charge for isoelectronic ions**

All have 10 electrons, but different numbers of protons pulling on them. More protons means greater effective nuclear charge and stronger attraction.

$$\text{protons: } S(16) > P(15) > Si(14) > Al(13)$$
The $S^{6+}$ ion also already has the highest positive charge, so repulsion is lowest and attraction per electron is greatest.

**Conclude the largest enthalpy change**

Removing a 2p electron from $S^{6+}$ needs the most energy, so the 7th ionisation energy of sulfur is the largest of the four processes.

options.A: This is the 4th ionisation energy of Al, removing a 2p electron from $Al^{3+}$. It is large, but $Al^{3+}$ has only 13 protons pulling on 10 electrons, the smallest nuclear charge here, so it is the easiest of the four.
options.B: This is the 6th ionisation energy of P, removing a 2p electron from $P^{5+}$. With 15 protons it is harder than Al and Si, but still has one proton fewer than S, so it is smaller than the sulfur process.
options.C: This is the 7th ionisation energy of S, $S^{6+}(g) \rightarrow S^{7+}(g) + e^-$. Starting from the isoelectronic $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ core, S has the most protons (16) and the highest starting charge (6+), giving the strongest attraction and the largest endothermic enthalpy change.
options.D: This is the 5th ionisation energy of Si, removing a 2p electron from $Si^{4+}$. With 14 protons it is harder than Al but easier than P and S, so students who focus only on breaking the neon octet miss the nuclear charge trend.
